claims.text: The starting material is a powder mixture containing Nb, Mo, Ta, W, V and Group IV elements such as Ti or Zr supplied as hydrides.
Oxygen introduced during preparation of NbMoTaWVTi can produce TiO precipitates in a BCC matrix.
Oxygen uptake in these alloys causes brittle alpha-HCP precipitation and raises the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.
Rapid heating to 800–900°C bypasses an oxygen-sensitive temperature window during hydride decomposition.
Processing below 10^-7 Pa, or at oxygen partial pressure below 10^-9 atm, is required to suppress oxygen uptake.
Minimizing dwell time at intermediate temperatures prevents significant oxygen diffusion.
Large deformation can refine the microstructure of a Group-IV-containing refractory HEA.
A high extrusion strain rate promotes dynamic recrystallization and densification.
Rapid hydrogen removal and oxygen exclusion stabilize a metastable BCC solid solution.
Rapid hydrogen removal and oxygen exclusion prevent alpha-HCP, TiO and TiO2 nucleation.
Thermal decomposition of TiH2 or ZrH2 releases hydrogen that can generate porosity if it is not evacuated.
Vacuum extrusion evacuates evolved hydrogen before oxygen can react with the Group IV elements.
High extrusion strain rate suppresses diffusion-controlled alpha-HCP precipitation.
Brittle oxide inclusions act as crack-initiation sites in the proposed alloy.
Low-oxygen powder feedstock is more promising than higher-oxygen powder routes for processing Group-IV-containing refractory HEAs.
The proposed extrusion route will produce material exceeding 99% theoretical density.
The proposed extrusion route will avoid catastrophic cracking.
The consolidated product will retain a single-phase BCC microstructure or only controlled nanoscale precipitates.
The product will have yield strength above 1000 MPa at 1000°C.
Conventionally arc-melted refractory HEAs can exhibit room-temperature plasticity below 2%.

contradictions.description: The environmental requirement is inconsistent: some fields require ultra-high vacuum below 10^-7 Pa, while others allow inert gas below 10^-9 atm O2 or argon below 1 ppm O2. One ppm is approximately 10^-6 atm and therefore does not satisfy the stated 10^-9 atm limit.

The causal narrative associates oxygen and brittle phases with an increased ductile-to-brittle transition temperature, yet the predicted benefit of preventing those phases is a significantly elevated transition temperature. Under the hypothesis's own framing, suppression of embrittlement should instead lower the transition temperature.
